Series::nansum¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::nansum() const -> Series
Series::nansum(std::int64_t dim) const -> Series
Series::nansum(std::int64_t dim, bool keepdim) const -> Series

What It Does¶

nansum() adds up the values along an axis, treating every NaN as 0.

It is the missing-data version of sum(): where sum() returns NaN the moment a single NaN enters the total, nansum() skips those positions and totals the rest. A reduced axis with no finite values at all sums to 0.

The no-argument form totals the whole series to a scalar. The dim forms reduce one axis, with keepdim controlling whether it is kept as a length-1 dimension.

Parameters¶

dim (std::int64_t, optional)

The axis to reduce. Negative values count from the back. Omitted: reduce everything to a scalar.

keepdim (bool, default false)

Keep the reduced axis as size 1 instead of removing it.

Returns¶

Series The NaN-skipping total. A scalar for the no-argument form; otherwise the input shape with dim removed (or kept as 1). An all-NaN reduced axis gives 0.

Gradient¶

nansum() is differentiable. The backward carries the upstream sensitivity to every finite position and 0 to the NaN positions:

d/dx_i nansum(x) = 0 if x_i is NaN, else 1

This is the behavior you want for masked or missing data — the skipped entries receive no gradient rather than a NaN one.

Examples¶

Example 1. NaN entries are skipped, not propagated.

double nan = std::nan("");

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({1.0, nan, 3.0, nan, 5.0}).nansum());

Output¶

Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=9.0000

1 + 3 + 5 = 9. Plain sum() here would be NaN.

Example 2. A reduced axis with no finite values sums to 0.

double nan = std::nan("");

pluss::series::print(std::cout, pluss::make_series({nan, nan}).nansum());

Output¶

Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=0.0000

Example 3. Reducing one axis of a matrix.

double nan = std::nan("");
auto m = pluss::make_series({{1.0, nan}, {3.0, 4.0}});

pluss::series::print(std::cout, m.nansum(0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[4.0000, 4.0000]

Column 0 is 1 + 3; column 1 skips the NaN and keeps just 4.

Example 4. The backward carries 1 to finite positions and 0 to NaN positions.

double nan = std::nan("");
auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, nan, 3.0, 5.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

x.nansum().reverse();

std::cout << "dx=" << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

dx=pluss::Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 0, 1, 1]

The NaN position gets 0; every finite position gets the upstream 1.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • nansum() of an all-NaN axis is 0, which is indistinguishable from a finite total that happens to be 0. Pair it with a count if you need to tell them apart.

  • +inf and -inf are not skipped; only NaN is.

  • Floating-point input.

Summary¶

nansum(x) totals an axis with NaN treated as 0:

  • all-NaN axis reduces to 0

  • dim / keepdim behave like the other reductions

  • differentiable, backward is 1 on finite positions and 0 on NaN positions

See Also¶

  • Series::sum: the plain total, which returns NaN on any NaN input.

  • Series::nanmean: the NaN-skipping average.

  • Series::nan_to_num: replace NaN (and infinities) explicitly before an ordinary reduction.
